topics.title: Iron: Absorption and bioavailability
topics.context: You can eat plenty of iron and still run low, because what counts is how much your gut actually lets in. Iron from meat and fish (heme) is absorbed far more easily than iron from plants (non-heme), and the rest of your plate can boost or block it. Knowing the rules turns “eat more spinach” into a real strategy, especially if you menstruate.
takeaways: From a mixed diet you absorb roughly 14–18% of the iron you eat; from a vegetarian diet, closer to 5–12%.
Vitamin C in the same meal (citrus, peppers, tomatoes) noticeably boosts how much plant iron you absorb.
Tea, coffee and calcium can get in the way, so enjoy them between meals rather than alongside your iron-rich ones.
A hormone called hepcidin rises after an iron dose, which is why some studies find alternate-day supplements absorb better. Check with a doctor before supplementing.

topics.title: Luteal phase: What your body asks for
topics.context: The luteal phase is the stretch between ovulation and your period, usually about two weeks, when progesterone takes the lead. Many people notice their hunger, sleep and mood shift here, and that’s physiology rather than a lack of willpower. Understanding it helps you plan meals, training and even your calendar with your body instead of against it.
takeaways: In a study of over 600,000 tracked cycles, the luteal phase averaged about 12 days, with real variation between people.
Progesterone nudges your resting body temperature up by a few tenths of a degree, which is what temperature-based cycle tracking picks up.
Calcium has some of the better evidence for easing PMS symptoms; ask a clinician before starting any supplement.
Sleep can get lighter in the days before your period, so a calm wind-down routine pays off most then.

topics.title: Doomscrolling: Why bad news is so sticky
topics.context: Ever opened your phone for one thing and surfaced forty minutes later, a little more anxious? Our brains give threats extra weight (the negativity bias), and endless feeds with unpredictable rewards lean right into that. Once you can see the mechanism, it gets much easier to design your way out of it.
takeaways: Negative information tends to grab more attention and linger longer in memory than positive information of the same size.
Unpredictable rewards, like the occasional great post, keep you swiping in the same way a slot machine does.
After the 2013 Boston Marathon bombing, people who watched hours of coverage reported more acute stress than some who were actually there.
Friction works: move apps off your home screen, log out, or set a stopping cue such as “one article, then close”.

topics.title: Stoicism: The dichotomy of control
topics.context: Nearly two thousand years ago, Epictetus, who was born enslaved and became a famous teacher, built a philosophy around one question: is this up to me or not? Sorting your worries into those two piles is surprisingly calming, and the idea later helped inspire modern cognitive therapies. It’s less about hiding feelings and more about putting your energy where it can actually land.
takeaways: Your judgments, intentions and actions are up to you; outcomes, other people and your reputation are not.
The Stoics weren’t emotionless. They examined the beliefs underneath their emotions.
Seneca describes an evening review: what went well today, what didn’t, and what you’d do differently.
Albert Ellis, a founder of cognitive behavioral approaches, named Epictetus as an influence.

topics.title: Inflation: Why your money quietly shrinks
topics.context: Inflation is the slow rise in prices that means the same money buys a little less each year. It sounds small, but at a steady 3% prices roughly double in about 24 years, so cash sitting still is quietly losing value. Understanding it helps you read the news, negotiate your salary and decide where your savings should live.
takeaways: The rule of 72: divide 72 by the inflation rate to estimate how many years it takes prices to double.
Your real return is roughly your interest rate minus inflation, so 5% savings with 4% inflation is only about 1% of real growth.
Many central banks aim for low, stable inflation and raise interest rates when prices run hot.
A raise smaller than inflation is a pay cut in disguise, which is useful to know before a salary talk.

topics.title: Scaling laws: Why bigger models got smarter
topics.context: In 2020, researchers found that language models improve in a surprisingly smooth, predictable way as you add parameters, data and compute. That finding helped justify the enormous training runs behind today’s LLMs, and a 2022 follow-up showed many models had been trained on too little data for their size. It’s the closest thing AI has to a law of physics, with real limits and lively debates.
takeaways: Loss falls as a power law with model size, data and compute, so on log-scale axes the trend looks like a straight line.
DeepMind’s Chinchilla work suggested scaling training data alongside model size, roughly 20 tokens per parameter.
Some “emergent” abilities may partly reflect how we measure them rather than sudden leaps.
Scaling predicts average performance well, but not exactly which skills appear or when.

topics.title: GDPR: Your right to see your data
topics.context: Under Europe’s GDPR, you can ask a company what personal data it holds about you, why it has it and who it shares it with, and it generally has one month to answer. It’s one of the most powerful and least used privacy tools around, and it has inspired similar laws worldwide, including Vietnam’s own personal data rules. Knowing how to use it turns vague privacy worries into concrete answers.
takeaways: Article 15 gives you a copy of your data plus details on why it’s used, who receives it and how long it’s kept.
A request is usually free and can be a plain email; no special form is required.
Companies normally have one month to reply, which can be extended by two more for complex requests.
Vietnam’s Decree 13/2023 on personal data protection borrows several GDPR ideas, including rights over your own data.

topics.title: Circadian rhythm: Why morning light matters
topics.context: Your body runs on a roughly 24-hour clock that times sleepiness, hormones, digestion and body temperature. Light is the strongest signal that sets that clock, which is why bright mornings and dim evenings can make falling asleep easier. It’s one of the few sleep tips that’s both free and well supported by research.
takeaways: A master clock in the brain, the suprachiasmatic nucleus, keeps clocks in the rest of the body in sync.
Light in the morning shifts your clock earlier; bright light late at night pushes it later.
Melatonin rises as evening darkens and works more as a “it’s night” signal than a knockout pill.
A consistent wake-up time anchors your rhythm, even more than a perfect bedtime.

topics.title: Attention residue: The hidden cost of switching
topics.context: When you jump from one task to another, part of your attention stays stuck on the first one. Researcher Sophie Leroy called this attention residue, and it explains why a “quick look” at messages can leave you foggy for much longer than the look itself. Designing longer, cleaner blocks of focus is one of the simplest upgrades you can make to your day.
takeaways: Leaving a task unfinished tends to create more residue than wrapping it up before you switch.
Jotting a quick “ready to resume” note (where you are, what’s next) helped people let go of an interrupted task in Leroy’s later research.
Batching email and chat into set windows keeps residue from leaking into your deep work.
Interrupted work often gets done faster but with more stress, so speed isn’t the whole story.

topics.title: Willpower: The ego depletion debate
topics.context: For years, a famous idea said willpower is like a muscle that tires with use, so resisting cookies in the morning leaves you weaker by evening. Then large replication projects struggled to find the effect, and the story got more interesting. What’s emerging instead is that beliefs, motivation and a well-designed environment may matter more than a fixed tank of self-control.
takeaways: The original 1998 ego depletion studies inspired hundreds of follow-ups before the doubts set in.
A 2016 replication across 23 labs found an effect close to zero.
In some studies, people who believed willpower isn’t easily used up showed little or no depletion.
People who seem most self-controlled often lean less on willpower and more on avoiding temptation in the first place.

topics.title: Index funds: Why boring investing often wins
topics.context: An index fund simply buys everything in a market index instead of trying to pick winners. Because most professional stock pickers fail to beat their benchmark over long periods, especially after fees, low-cost index investing has become standard advice for everyday savers. It’s worth understanding the logic and its limits before putting money anywhere. This is general education, not financial advice.
takeaways: S&P’s SPIVA reports keep finding that most actively managed funds trail their index over 10 to 15 years.
Fees compound too: a 1% yearly fee can quietly take a large slice of long-term returns.
Spreading money across a whole market lowers single-company risk, but index funds still fall when the whole market does.
What’s available depends on where you live, so compare fees, currency and tax rules before choosing.

topics.title: Gut–brain axis: Your second brain
topics.context: Your gut has its own nervous system, and it’s in constant conversation with your brain through the vagus nerve, hormones, immune signals and the trillions of microbes living there. Research over the past two decades suggests this link may shape stress and mood, though much of the strongest evidence still comes from animal studies. It’s one of the most exciting, and most over-hyped, areas in biology right now.
takeaways: The enteric nervous system has hundreds of millions of neurons, which is why it’s nicknamed the second brain.
Most of the body’s serotonin is made in the gut, although that serotonin doesn’t cross into the brain directly.
Mice raised without gut microbes show exaggerated stress responses; human evidence is promising but earlier-stage.
A varied, fiber-rich diet feeds a more diverse microbiome, a sensible habit whatever the hype.
